D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b000_.text: In the last video, I told you about the drawer top right in my desk in the finance office at Bird Road Auto Plaza. Today, I'm opening it. You're sitting in a little room with no windows. There's a framed picture of a sailboat on the wall and a bowl of mints, and the air conditioning is a little too cold on purpose. Across the desk, there's a man in a nice tie with gray hair, like a grandson's favorite uncle. He's smiling. He says, this will just take a few minutes. And he slides a piece of paper across the desk, and he turns it so it faces you. And in that moment, before you read one word, three tricks have already started. I know, because I'm the man with the gray hair. I sat in that chair for 26 years. My name is Hector. I sold cars in Miami for 40 years, 14 on the lot, 26 in the box, the Finance and Insurance Office, F&I, at Bird Road Auto Plaza.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b001_.text: Today I'm going to show you the 10 tricks I kept in that drawer. The ones I used on retirees more than anybody, because retirees are polite and retirees trust a man with gray hair. For every trick, I'll tell you who I used it on, what it cost them, and the exact words to stop it. And the 10th one is the one I used on Mrs. Dottie Shapiro in 1988. The one nobody catches. Stay for that one. First, the drawer. Let me tell you what was in it. A stack of menus, a heavy gold pen, a nice one, the kind that makes you feel important when you sign, a rate sheet from every bank we worked with, face down, always face down, and a little calculator, a gray one, with big buttons. I never let the customer see the screen, never. Abe Feldman, the man who taught me this business in 1975, gave me that rule. He said, Hector, the customer sees the answer, never the arithmetic.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b002_.text: Okay, trick number one, the menu. You know those restaurants where they put three bottles of wine on the table? The cheap one, the expensive one, and the one in the middle? Everybody buys the one in the middle. We did the same thing with a piece of paper. The menu had three columns, sometimes four. At the top, the names, platinum, gold, preferred. And at the bottom, under each column, a monthly payment. Platinum had everything. The seven year service contract, the gap, the tire and wheel, the paint and fabric protection, the key replacement, the dent repair. Gold had a little less. Preferred had a little less. And then in the last column, way on the right, in small letters, basic, just the car. And the payment on the basic was, of course, the smallest. But the way I presented it, my finger started on platinum, always. I read every item in platinum slowly, like a poem.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b003_.text: And by the time my finger got to basic, basic sounded naked. Basic sounded like you didn't love your family. And people, nice people, chose gold. Gold was usually about $2,500 to $3,000 of products in the middle. Like the wine. So when I put a menu in front of you, here's what you say. And you say it before I start reading. I like the payment for the car only, with nothing added. Then I'll decide if I want anything. that's it you start from zero not from platinum from zero everything is something you're adding and you'll see the price of each one by itself trick number two the payment that already had the products inside this one's quieter and it's the reason i'm sitting here honestly because it's the one i'm most ashamed of before you came into my office the salesman would have told you a payment

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b004_.text: Let's say $489 a month. You agreed. You shook his hand. Now you come to me. And sometimes, not always, but sometimes the $489 was already a little high. The real payment for the car alone was $445. The salesman quoted high on purpose. We call that a leg. Leaving a leg in the payment. So when I showed you the menu, I could say, Good news, Mr. Goh, with the preferred package, your payment is still $489. Nothing changes. You're protected for seven years and your payment is exactly what you agreed to. And people said, oh, that's wonderful because their payment didn't change. They didn't see that they just bought $1,500 of products with money they thought was the car. 1993, Mr. Sid Gold, retired tailor from North Miami Beach, 76 years old,

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b005_.text: Beautiful suit every day, even in August. He used to measure people with his eyes. He came into the box. I did the leg and he looked at me for a long time and he said, Hector, I've been measuring men my whole life. You just took something in at the waist and I laughed and he signed anyway. He knew he signed anyway because he was tired. That's the other trick. The time. I'll get to the time. So what do you say? Before you leave the salesman's desk, you ask for the payment with nothing added, written down, and the number of months. Then in the box you ask, what is the payment for the car alone with nothing added? And you compare it to the paper. If the box gives you a different number than the desk, the difference is the leg. And now you know. Trick number three. The rate sheet face down. I told you about this in the first video, briefly. Let me open it up now.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b006_.text: On my desk, there were sheets from the banks. Every bank tells the dealer, for a customer with this credit score for this many months, we'll buy the loan at this rate. That's the buy rate. And the dealer is allowed to add on top, usually up to two or two and a half points, and keep a big part of the difference. That was my paycheck. Literally. A big piece of what I made every month came from that difference. 1998. A retired fireman from Kendall. Credit score. Beautiful. over 800. The bank said 4.9. I told him 6.9. He said, Hector, that's very good. My brother-in-law got eight on a $25,000 loan for 60 months. Those two points were about $1,300 for him to pay to us. And he left happy because his brother-in-law got eight. So how do you stop it? Two ways.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b007_.text: The first, I told you, is a pre-approval from your own credit union before you walk in. The second, you ask, in the box, out loud, these words. What is the buy rate the bank approved me at? Some finance managers will tell you. Some will dance. But the moment you say the words buy rate, he knows you know. And a finance manager who knows you know will usually come down. I always came down. It's like a dog that sees the leash. Trick number four, the bank called back. This is the nastiest one in the drawer. And I want to tell you the truth. I did this twice in my career and both times our general manager made me do it and I stopped doing it the third time he asked. That's not an excuse, it's just the truth. Here's how it works. You buy the car on a Saturday. The dealer lets you drive it home that night even though the bank hasn't actually approved the loan yet. They call it spot delivery.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b008_.text: Delivery on the spot. And you sign a paper in the stack that says if the financing doesn't go through, the dealer can cancel the deal. And a week later the phone rings. Mr. Pierre, it's Hector at Bird Road. I'm sorry, the bank didn't approve the loan at the rate we discussed. You need to come in and sign a new contract at a higher rate. 2002. Mr. Raymond Pierre, retired taxi driver from Little Haiti off Northeast 2nd Avenue. 30 years driving a cab in Miami. He knew every street. He'd already sold his old car to his neighbor because we told him the deal was done. So when the phone rang, he had no car to go back to He came in, sat in my chair, and he signed it two points higher And he said in that soft voice, I thought it was done, Mr. Hector I thought when you sign, it's done And I said, I'm sorry, and I meant it, and I did it anyway

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b009_.text: People call this yo-yo financing because the car goes out and comes back like a yo-yo. And in a lot of states, there are rules now about how long the dealer has to cancel and what he has to give back. But don't depend on the rules. Depend on this sentence. Before you drive away, you ask, is my financing final? Has the bank approved this contract or is this conditional? And if he says it's conditional, you have two choices. You leave the car there until it's final or you use your own credit union loan. And never, never sell or give away your old car until you know the new loan is final. Keep your old car in the garage one more week like Mr. Pierre should have. Let me stop for a second because I promised you Mrs. Shapiro and I'm going to tell you the next piece now before trick five. Because trick five is the one she asked me about. 1988 Coral Way Motors, Mrs.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b010_.text: Shapiro had put Irving's insurance check back in her purse because I told her to keep it as her cushion. And I slid the papers across the desk. And she looked at the papers for a long time. She had little gold reading glasses on a chain around her neck. And she said, Hector, Irving had a thing for the old car, a warranty. He always said, Dottie, if the car brakes were covered, do I need one of those? Will I be covered? And I didn't answer right away. I let the question sit there. Abe taught me that too. When a customer asked you a question, wait, let her hear her own fear. And then I said, Mrs. Shapiro, that's a very good question. And I opened the drawer. What I took out of that drawer, I'll tell you in the next video with the number. I promised you I would tell this in pieces and I'm keeping my promise. Trick number five, fear. The transmission speech.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b011_.text: Every finance manager in America has a speech. Mine was about the transmission. I could do it in my sleep. Mr. Jones, do you know what a transmission costs today? I'd lean back, $4,000, $5,000. And on these new cars, with all the computers, one sensor, one little sensor, $800. And then I'd look at his wife. And on a fixed income, Mrs. Jones, that's a lot of money to find all at once. and she'd look at him and he'd look at me and that was the service contract. Seven years, a hundred thousand miles, $2,400. Now here's what I didn't say. A service contract, an extended warranty. Sometimes it makes sense for some cars, for some people. If you're going to keep the car long time, if you drive a lot, but here's the insider part. The price of that contract is not fixed.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b012_.text: The dealer buys it from the company for a certain amount, and the price to you is whatever I could get. Sometimes we doubled it. On a $2,400 contract, the real cost might be $1,200. So three sentences. First, I'm not buying it today. Most of these contracts can be bought later, any time before the factory warranty ends. So you can go home and think. Second, if you want one, what's your cost on this contract? I'd like to pay closer to your cost. He won't tell you the cost, but he'll come down a lot. And third, and this is the one nobody knows, most of these contracts can be canceled later and you get a refund for the time you didn't use. So if you bought one last year in a moment of fear, it's not too late. Call the dealer, ask for the cancellation form, and read what it says about the refund. Trick number six, the gap with a big price, gap insurance.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b013_.text: Some of you know what it is if your car is stolen or totaled in an accident. Your regular insurance pays what the car is worth that day. But if you owe more on the loan than the car is worth, that difference is the gap. And gap insurance pays it. Gap is not a scam. Sometimes it's smart. If you put very little down, if you have a long loan, if you rolled an old balance into the new one, you can owe more than the car is worth for years. but at the dealership I sold Gap for six, seven, eight hundred dollars and more inside the payment and the same coverage from a lot of auto insurance companies you can add to your regular policy for a few dollars a month and many credit unions sell it for a few hundred. 2009 a couple from Hialeah Gardens both retired from the post office. They put down $12,000 on a $22,000 car. $12,000 down

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b014_.text: They didn't need Gap. They would never owe more than the car was worth. And I sold them Gap for $7.95 because it was on the menu and my finger started on platinum. So the sentence, how much do I owe compared to what the car is worth? If you put a big down payment, you probably don't need Gap. And if you do need it, you say, I'll get it through my insurance company. Then call your insurance agent the same afternoon and ask what it costs. You'll laugh. Trick number seven, insurance for the loan if you die. This one, I want the retirees to listen very carefully, because this one was for you, only for you, almost. In the 80s and 90s, it was huge. Credit life insurance, it pays off the car loan if you die, and credit disability, it makes the payments if you get sick or hurt.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b015_.text: And in the box, I look at the husband, a man 70, 72 years old. And I say softly, Mr. Gonzalez, if something happens to you, God forbid, do you want Mrs. Gonzalez to have a car payment on top of everything? And he will look at her and she will look at the floor. And he signed every time. It was the easiest signature in the business. 1990, Bird Road. I sold credit life to a retired man from Westchester. He lived three blocks from me. I saw him at the bakery every Sunday. And that coverage cost him more than a regular life insurance policy would have cost for the same amount. Because the price was built into the loan and we got a commission on it. And for years I saw him at the bakery, buying pastelitos, and I couldn't look him in the eye. So the sentence, I already have life insurance, thank you. Or, if you don't, I'll look into it with my own agent.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b016_.text: And if the finance man says, it's only $12 a month, you remember, $12 a month on a six-year loan is $864. For something you can probably get cheaper or something you don't need at all. If there's money in the estate to pay off a small car loan. Okay, let me give you a word about the clock. Because the clock is a trick all by itself. And it's in every one of the ten. By the time you get to the box, you've been at the dealership three, four, sometimes five hours. You've had two coffees and no lunch. You're 74 years old. Your back hurts from that little plastic chair on the showroom floor. And I knew that. That's why the box is at the end. Nobody makes good decisions at hour four. Not me, not you, not a judge. So here's the trick to beat the trick. Go in the morning, right when they open. Eat something before.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b017_.text: Bring a bottle of water and a granola bar in your bag. And if it passes three hours, you say, I'm tired. I'll come back tomorrow to sign. The paper will be there tomorrow, I promise. Trick number eight, the calculator I never showed you. Pennies a day, that was the language. I never said, this service contract is $1,800. I said, Mrs. Fuentes, it's about 80 cents a day, less than your cafecito at the Versailles. And it's true, more or less. $1,800 divided by 72 months divided by 30 days is about 83 cents a day but $1,800 is $1,800 plus interest because it's inside the loan so you pay interest on it for six years and the calculator the gray one I would type numbers turn it toward me look at it nod and say a number and the customer never saw what I typed sometimes I round it up

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b018_.text: Sometimes I added a little. It was not illegal, exactly, because the real numbers were on the contract. But the customer believed the calculator, not the contract, because the man with gray hair was holding the calculator. So the sentence, what's the total price of that product, by itself, in dollars, not per month, not per day, the total. And if he types on a calculator you say nicely Can I see that? Turn it around Or better bring your own A $5 calculator from the drugstore Big buttons in your purse When you take out your own calculator Believe me The man across the desk sits up straight I always did Trick number nine The bank requires it This is the lie Plain and simple I'll say it This is the one I'm talking about When people say car dealers lie Not every finance manager does it, but I worked with men who did, and I heard it through the wall many times. Mr.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b019_.text: Lopez, I'm sorry, with your credit, the bank is going to require the service contract to approve the loan, or the bank requires gap, or to get this rate, the bank requires the protection package. And the customer thinks, well, if the bank requires it, I have no choice. In general, for a regular car loan, the bank does not require you to buy a service contract or a paint package to approve you. It's the dealer who wants it. And telling you a product is required when it isn't, that's the kind of thing regulators have gone after dealers for more than once. So the sentence, and it's a beautiful sentence, use it. Please show me in writing where the bank requires that and then stop talking. He'll look at you. He'll say something about policy and you say it again. Please show me in writing. You will be amazed how fast that requirement disappears like magic.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b020_.text: like the man in the cigar shop on Calle Ocho who made a coin disappear for the kids. Now before number 10, let me tell you about Mrs. Shapiro's hand, because that's what number 10 is about, her hand. That afternoon, in 1988, after I'd opened the drawer and taken out what I took out, I had a stack of papers, contract, credit application, title application, odometer statement, the buyer's order, and the products. And she had that gold pen in her hand, Irving's pen actually. She had it in her purse. It was his. And I started turning the pages. Sign here, an initial here, and here, and here, Mrs. Shapiro, 14 signatures. I counted them later, years later, when I found the copy in an old box in my garage. 14. and while she signed, I talked about her grandchildren in New Jersey, about the weather, about Irving, and her hand just kept signing.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b021_.text: She never read one page, not one, and I never stopped talking long enough for her to. Trick number 10, the one nobody catches, the signing ceremony. That's what we called it, joking. The ceremony, because it was like a ritual. The finance manager turns the pages, puts his finger where you sign, and talks the whole time. Little yellow sticky flags that say sign here. and the customer tired trusting signs where the finger is and somewhere in the stack a page you never saw a product you said no to that ended up in there anyway a number of months that's different from what the salesman said a rate that's one point higher than the one I told you out loud most people think the danger in the box is the speech the menu the fear the transmission that's not where it is. The danger is the five minutes at the end when you're signing and he's talking. So here's what nobody does.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b022_.text: Before you sign anything, you put the pen down. You literally put the pen on the desk. And you say, I'm going to read the contract now. Please give me a few minutes. And then you look for one box. On every car loan contract in America, by federal law, the truth in lending law, there is a box with four numbers. The annual percentage rate, the APR, the finance charge, the total interest in dollars, the amount financed, and the total of payments, those four numbers. You check three things. One, is the APR the rate he said out loud? Two, is the number of payments the number of months you agreed to? 60 is 60, not 72. And three, look for the itemization, the list of what's in the amount financed. Every product is there with its price. If you said no to something and it's on that list, you point at it and you say, I said no to this. Please take it out and print a new contract.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b023_.text: and you wait, however long it takes. I promise you it takes four minutes to print a new contract. I did it a thousand times. And while you're reading, he'll talk. He'll talk about your grandchildren. You say nicely, give me a moment, I'm reading. That's all. That's the whole trick to beat the ceremony. Put the pen down, read the box, say I'm reading. And my nephew Danny says, the ceremony has changed. Today, at a lot of dealerships, there's no stack of paper, there's a tablet or a little signing pad with a plastic pen on a cord like at the pharmacy and The finance manager says okay sign here once and it's going to apply your signature to all the documents One signature 14 pages you never even see them go by Danny says it's faster for everybody and it is but faster is not your friend in that room and

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b024_.text: So you say, before I sign, I'd like to see each document on the screen or a printed copy, every page. You have the right to see what you're signing. And when you get home, ask them to email you a copy of everything, the whole contract with the box of four numbers. Keep it in the folder with your title. And while we're at it, a little bonus, number 11, because Danny told me this one is everywhere now. the prepaid maintenance plan. We'll do all your oil changes for three years, $899. Sounds nice, but count it. An oil change on most new cars is every seven, 10,000 miles. A retiree driving to Publix and to church and to the doctor, maybe 6,000 miles a year. That's two oil changes a year, maybe. Six over three years. At the dealer's own service price, that might be four or $500. dollars. You're paying almost double inside the loan with interest.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b025_.text: And if you move to Ocala to be near the grandkids, good luck using it. So the sentence, I'll pay for my oil changes when I need them. Thank you. Now, what if you already signed? What if you're watching this and you're thinking, Hector, that was me. Last spring, I bought the gold package. Don't feel bad. Smart people bought my gold package for 26 years. Here's what you do. Find your contract. Look for the itemization. the list, write down every product and its price. Then for each one, the service contract, the gap, the tire and wheel, the maintenance plan. Look at the back of that product's own paper for the word cancellation. Most of them can be canceled and you get back the part you didn't use, sometimes minus a small fee. If the loan is still open, the refund usually goes to the loan and your balance goes down.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b026_.text: You call the dealer's finance office and you say, I'd like to cancel these products. Please send me the cancellation forms. If they drag their feet, and some will, you can call the company that issued the contract directly. Their phone number is on the paper. And if someone lied to you, if they told you the bank required something, you can file a complaint with your state attorney general's office. They take those seriously, more than you think. Let me give you the 10 again, quick. Get your index card. 1. The menu? Say, the payment for the car only, nothing added, start from zero. 2. The leg in the payment? Get the payment with nothing added and writing from the salesman, and compare it in the box. 3. The rate sheet? Ask, what's the buy rate the bank approved me at? Or bring your credit union letter. 4. The bank call back? Ask, is my financing final?

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b027_.text: And keep your old car until it is. 5. The transmission speech. Not today. What's your cost? And you can cancel later for a refund. 6. Gap with a big price. If you put a lot down, you may not need it. If you do, call your insurance agent. 7. Insurance on the loan if you die. I'll check with my own agent. 8. Pennies a day and the hidden calculator. What's the total in dollars? And bring your own calculator. 9. The bank requires it. Show me in writing. 10. The signing ceremony. Put the pen down. Read the truth in lending box. I'm reading. And the clock. Go in the morning, eat before. And if it passes three hours, come back tomorrow. You know when I retired in 2015, they gave me a little party at Bird Road. A cake from the Cuban bakery, with a car on it made of frosting and on my last day I cleaned out the drawer. The menus went in the trash.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b028_.text: The rate sheets went in the shred box, the gray calculator I left for the young man taking my place, and the gold pen, the heavy one I took home. I have it on my desk right now. Marisol asked me once why I kept it, and I told her the truth, so I don't forget how heavy it was. Now, Mrs. Shapiro asked me that question, will I be covered? And I opened the drawer. What came out of that drawer was a piece of paper with a price on it, and the price was not the price. In the next video I'm going to tell you 7 fees I charge seniors, 7 real lines on a real buyer's order that you can refuse, out loud, at the desk, with one sentence each. And I'll tell you finally the number, what I put in Mrs. Shapiro's payment, and how much it cost her every single month. Subscribe so you don't miss it. And tell me in the comments, what did the finance manager tell you was required, the exact words.

D:\\wt\\enhc03\\vlog\\enhc03\\voz\\b029_.text: I'll tell you if it's true. I read every single one with my coffee every morning. Marisol says I'm finally doing honest work. I'll see you in the box.
